Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

derivations.claim: Continuity and attainment in [F2] show that $S_+\cup S_-$ is nonempty and compact: the maximum of $|e|$ is attained and $E>0$, while each level set is closed in the compact interval [F1]. If one of $S_+$ or $S_-$ is empty, take $h=1$ or $h=-1$ according to the sign of the nonempty set; this has degree zero and the required sign.

Suppose both sets are nonempty. Their product is a closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R^2$, so [F2] applied to the continuous distance function gives a minimum separation $\delta=\min\{|x-y|:x\in S_+,\,y\in S_-\}>0$; it is positive because the two compact sets are disjoint. Starting at the leftmost point of $S_+\cup S_-$, repeatedly take the first point of the opposite-sign set to the right and the last current-sign point before it. These extrema exist because the level sets are compact, and each transition gives an open gap of length at least $\delta$ containing no point of $S_+\cup S_-$. The process therefore has finitely many transitions, each with a distinct ordered gap.

If there were at least $n+1$ transitions, choosing one extremal point from each successive sign run would give $n+2$ ordered alternating points, contrary to the hypothesis. Thus the number $k$ of transitions is at most $n$. Choose one point $\xi_j$ in each transition gap and set $h(x)=c\prod_{j=1}^{k}(x-\xi_j)$, where $c\in\{-1,1\}$ is chosen so that $h$ has the sign of $e$ on the first run. The polynomial has degree $k\le n$, has no zero on $S_+\cup S_-$, and changes sign exactly when the extremal sign changes. Hence $e(x)h(x)>0$ on the entire extremal set.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

For nonzero $p=(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$, define $\deg p:=n$ and $\operatorname{lc}(p):=a_n$. The zero polynomial has no degree and no leading coefficient. Let $F$ be a field and let $f,g\in F[x]$ be not both zero. Repeated polynomial division terminates at a last nonzero remainder, whose monic associate is $d=\gcd(f,g)$. There are $A,B\in F[x]$ such that

$$ Af+Bg=d. $$

Moreover, $d$ divides both $f$ and $g$, and every common divisor of $f$ and $g$ divides $d$.

derivations.claim: For a nonzero quotient, let $d=\gcd(p,q)$ from [F1] and put $p_0=p/d$, $q_0=q/d$. Then $Ap+Bq=d$ implies $Ap_0+Bq_0=1$, so no nonconstant polynomial divides both $p_0$ and $q_0$. For the zero quotient, $p=0$ and reducing by $\gcd(0,q)$ gives $(0,1)$.

Suppose $p_0/q_0=p_1/q_1$ are nonzero reduced representations. Cross-multiplication gives $p_0q_1=p_1q_0$. By the Bézout identity $Ap_0+Bq_0=1$ from step 1.1, multiplication by $p_1$ shows $p_0$ divides $p_1$; the same argument with the denominator gives $q_0\mid q_1$. Write $p_1=h p_0$ and $q_1=k q_0$. Cross-multiplication and nonzero $p_0q_0$ give $h=k$. If $h$ were nonconstant, it would divide both $p_1$ and $q_1$, contradicting reduction. Thus $h=k$ is a nonzero constant. The zero case is the reduced pair already identified in step 1.1.

If both positive denominators have coefficient norm $1$, their common scalar from step 2.1 is positive and its multiplication scales the coefficient norm by that scalar. The two norms being $1$ forces the scalar to be $1$, and then the numerators agree as well.

real-valued continuous functions on $I$. For $h\in C(I,\mathbb R)$ set

$\mathcal P_n(I)$ be the restrictions to $I$ of real polynomials of degree at
most $n$, including the zero polynomial, and define
$$E_n(f;I):=\inf_{p\in\mathcal P_n(I)}\|f-p\|_{\infty,I}.$$
When $I=[-1,1]$, this agrees with the published definition
[[def-best-uniform-polynomial-approximation-error-and-chebyshev-interpolants]].

continuous difference $f-p$ has a finite maximum absolute value. The

divisor, and
$$\|q\|_{\mathrm{coef},2}:=\left(\sum_{j=0}^{n}q_j^2\right)^{1/2}=1\quad\text{when }q(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}q_jx^j.$$

admissible under these conditions has exactly one normalized reduced pair.

$$\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I):=\{p/q:(p,q)\text{ is a normalized reduced pair}\}$$
and
$$E_{m,n}(f,w;I):=\inf_{r\in\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I)}\|w(f-r)\|_{\infty,I}.$$

$q>0$ on $I$ makes $r$ continuous by
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $w(f-r)$ is continuous and bounded

language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**

runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,

nonzero rational function differ by a common nonzero real scalar. The zero

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Now suppose $r$ is best with $E:=E_r>0$, and put $e=w(f-r)$. Its active-extrema set is compact. If it had no $N+2$ alternating points, [F4] would give a polynomial $g\in\mathcal P_N$ with $e(x)g(x)>0$ on that set. By [F3], choose $u,v$ with $\deg u\le m$, $\deg v\le n$, and $g=uq-pv$.

**Inputs.** A nondegenerate interval $I=[a,b]$, degrees $m,n\ge0$, continuous
real target $f$, strictly positive continuous weight $w$, a finite exchange
integer budget $B\in\mathbb N_0$, an initial reference of $m+n+2$ ordered distinct nodes, an
exact rational alternation-solver procedure, and an exact weighted-extrema
oracle.

The alternation solver is an explicit input procedure. On a reference
$X=(x_0,\ldots,x_{m+n+1})$, it solves the nonlinear equations
$$w(x_i)\bigl(f(x_i)-p(x_i)/q(x_i)\bigr)=(-1)^i\lambda$$
with $p,q$ coprime, $\deg p\le m$, $\deg q\le n$, $q>0$ on $I$, and
$\|q\|_{\mathrm{coef},2}=1$. It reports one of: a unique candidate with
defect $d=0$; an exact defective candidate with its computed $d>0$; singular
or nonunique system; no normal solution; or inconclusive. The procedure does
not assume that this nonlinear solve always succeeds.

The weighted-extrema oracle for a returned candidate $r=p/q$ reports one of:

- alternation$(E,Y)$ only when $E=\|w(f-r)\|_{\infty,I}$ and $Y$ consists of
  $N_{m,n}(r)+2$ ordered distinct points with weighted residuals
  $\sigma(-1)^iE$;
- maximum$(E,x)$ only when $E=\|w(f-r)\|_{\infty,I}$ and
  $|w(x)(f(x)-r(x))|=E$; or
- inconclusive.

**Procedure.** For $k=0,\ldots,B$, call the alternation solver on the current
reference. Return its singular, no-normal-solution, or inconclusive status
unchanged. If it returns a defective candidate, return
defective$(d,N_{m,n}(r))$ immediately; do not apply the normal
$m+n+2$-point count. For a normal candidate $(r,\lambda)$, query the
weighted-extrema oracle. An exact zero error returns exact$(r)$. An
alternation response with $E>0$ returns certified$(r,E,Y)$, with optimality supplied by
[[thm-na-weighted-rational-alternation-characterization]]. For maximum$(E,x)$
with $E=|\lambda|$, the current reference itself is an exact global
alternation certificate, so return certified$(r,E,X)$. If $\lambda=0<E$,
return zero-level-no-exchange. If $E>|\lambda|$,
exchange the returned maximum point $x$ for the smallest reference node $x_i$
whose expected sign $\operatorname{sgn}(\lambda)(-1)^i$ matches the sign of
$w(x)(f(x)-r(x))$ and for which replacing $x_i$ by $x$ preserves strict
ordering. If no such index exists, return no-valid-exchange. After $B+1$
unsuccessful iterations, return budget-exhausted.

**Outputs.** The procedure returns an exact minimax certificate, an exact
zero-error candidate, or an explicit defect, singularity, no-solution,
oracle, exchange, or budget status. It claims no existence of a successful
nonlinear solve and no iterative convergence.

Let $n\ge0$, let $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be any function,
and let $x_0<\cdots<x_{n+1}$ be distinct nodes in $I$. There is a unique pair
$(p,\lambda)\in\mathcal P_n(I)\times\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$p(x_i)+(-1)^i\lambda=f(x_i),\qquad 0\le i\le n+1.$$

**Inputs.** A nondegenerate interval $I=[a,b]$, a degree $n\ge0$, a continuous
real function $f$ on $I$, an integer exchange budget $B\in\mathbb N_0$, and an initial reference
$X=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n+1})$ with $a\le x_0<\cdots<x_{n+1}\le b$. Also supply an
exact extrema oracle for a polynomial candidate $p$. On each call it returns
one of:

- alternation$(E,y_0,\ldots,y_{n+1})$, only when $E=\|f-p\|_{\infty,I}$ and the
  returned ordered distinct nodes satisfy $f(y_i)-p(y_i)=\sigma(-1)^iE$ for
  one fixed sign $\sigma$;
- maximum$(E,y)$, only when $E=\|f-p\|_{\infty,I}$ and
  $|f(y)-p(y)|=E$; or
- inconclusive, when neither exact certificate can be returned.

**Procedure.** For $k=0,\ldots,B$, solve the unique real linear system
$$p_k(x_i)+(-1)^i\lambda_k=f(x_i),\qquad 0\le i\le n+1,$$
for $p_k\in\mathcal P_n(I)$ and $\lambda_k\in\mathbb R$, using
[[lem-na-polynomial-remez-system-invertible]]. Query the oracle for $p_k$.
If an exact oracle response certifies $E=0$, return exact$(p_k)$. If it returns
alternation$(E,Y)$ with $E>0$, return certified$(p_k,E,Y)$; the optimality
claim is discharged by [[thm-na-polynomial-equioscillation-certificate]]. If
it returns inconclusive, return oracle-inconclusive. If it returns
maximum$(E,y)$ with $E>0$ and $E=|\lambda_k|$, return certified$(p_k,E,X)$,
because the solved equations make $X$ an alternating set and the oracle
certifies the global norm. If $\lambda_k=0<E$, return zero-level-no-exchange.

In the remaining case, let $s=\operatorname{sgn}(f(y)-p_k(y))$. Find the
smallest index $i$ for which $s=\operatorname{sgn}(\lambda_k)(-1)^i$ and
$y$ lies strictly between the neighboring reference nodes (use $a$ as the
left neighbor at $i=0$ and $b$ as the right neighbor at $i=n+1$). Replace
$x_i$ by $y$ and continue. If no such index exists, return
no-order-preserving-exchange. If all $B+1$ iterations finish without a
certificate, return budget-exhausted with the last candidate and reference.

**Outputs.** The procedure returns an exact best-approximation certificate,
an exact zero-error candidate, or one of the explicit inconclusive,
zero-level, no-exchange, or budget statuses. It asserts no convergence of the
iterates. Any implementation must ensure each exact solve and oracle call
terminates.

Let $n\ge0$, let $f\in C([a,b],\mathbb R)$ with $a<b$, and let

that
$$f(x_i)-p(x_i)=\sigma(-1)^iE\qquad(0\le i\le n+1),$$
then no polynomial in $\mathcal P_n([a,b])$ has smaller uniform error than
$p$. Thus the displayed residual values are an a posteriori optimality
certificate.

Let $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, let $m,n\in\mathbb N_0$, and let
$f,w\in C(I,\mathbb R)$ with $w(x)>0$ for every $x\in I$. A normalized
reduced pair is a pair of real polynomials $p,q$ such that $q>0$ on $I$,
$\deg p\le m$, $\deg q\le n$, $p$ and $q$ have no nonconstant common
divisor, and
$$\|q\|_{\mathrm{coef},2}:=\left(\sum_{j=0}^{n}q_j^2\right)^{1/2}=1\quad\text{when }q(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}q_jx^j.$$
The zero rational function is represented by $(p,q)=(0,1)$. By
[[lem-na-reduced-rational-representation-unique]], each rational function
admissible under these conditions has exactly one normalized reduced pair.
Define
$$\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I):=\{p/q:(p,q)\text{ is a normalized reduced pair}\}$$
and
$$E_{m,n}(f,w;I):=\inf_{r\in\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I)}\|w(f-r)\|_{\infty,I}.$$
The family is nonempty because it contains $r=0$. For each admissible $r=p/q$,
$q>0$ on $I$ makes $r$ continuous by
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $w(f-r)$ is continuous and bounded
on compact $I$. The infimum is therefore finite, bounded below by zero, and
exists as a real number by completeness of $\mathbb R$.

For $r=p/q\ne0$ in reduced form, put
$$d_{m,n}(r):=\min\{m-\deg p,\ n-\deg q\},\qquad N_{m,n}(r):=m+n-d_{m,n}(r).$$
For $r=0$, define $d_{m,n}(0):=n$ and hence $N_{m,n}(0):=m$. The integer
$d_{m,n}(r)$ is the defect. A candidate is **normal** when $d_{m,n}(r)=0$
and **defective** when $d_{m,n}(r)>0$. The alternation count associated with
the candidate is $N_{m,n}(r)+2$; it equals $m+n+2$ only in the normal case.

Let $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, let $m,n\ge0$, and let $f,w\in C(I,\mathbb R)$
with $w>0$ on $I$. A best rational approximant in
$\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I)$ exists and is unique. For a candidate $r=p/q$ with
positive weighted error $E_r:=\|w(f-r)\|_{\infty,I}>0$, let
$N=N_{m,n}(r)=m+n-d_{m,n}(r)$. Then $r$ is best if and only if there are
$N+2$ ordered nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_{N+1}$ in $I$ and
$\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$ such that
$$w(x_i)(f(x_i)-r(x_i))=\sigma(-1)^iE_r\qquad(0\le i\le N+1).$$
If the best error is $0$, positivity of $w$ forces the unique best function
to be $f$ itself. In the normal case $d=0$ the count is $m+n+2$; for
defective candidates the count is $m+n+2-d$.
